distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer disease leaf for acute superficial infection of the upper dermis and superficial cutaneous lymphatics, with raised sharply demarcated erythema and lymphatic inflammation. The leaf is independent of anatomic site, recurrence status, organism, bullous or hemorrhagic morphology, bacteremia, shock, or treatment response.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: Cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, diabetic foot infection, deep abscess, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, streptococcal or staphylococcal bacteremia, toxic shock syndrome, generic sepsis, DRESS/SJS-TEN, zoster, DVT, gout, contact dermatitis, vasculitis, and carcinoma erysipeloides remain competing manifolds or complications/context. They are not appended to the disease name.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking should use observed raised sharply demarcated erythema, warmth, edema, tenderness, superficial induration, lymphangitis or regional lymphadenopathy, face/lower-limb/trunk site, portal context, lymphedema or venous insufficiency, fever/chills/malaise, vital signs, CBC, CRP/ESR/PCT, lactate, renal injury, bullae or hemorrhagic lesions, and superficial imaging when available. Culture species, susceptibility, final source adjudication, biopsy exclusion, and treatment response are confirmatory or post-workup context unless explicitly testing post-workup mode.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Skin portal and superficial lymphatic entry
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Minor trauma, fissure, interdigital maceration, tinea, ulcer, piercing, surgical scar, insect bite, chronic edema skin fragility, or an unapparent portal allows organisms to enter upper dermis and superficial lymphatics.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Superficial dermal and lymphatic pathogen burden
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Viable bacteria, usually beta-hemolytic streptococci but sometimes staphylococci or Gram-negative organisms in selected hosts, proliferate in upper dermis and superficial lymphatics.

Neutrophil, complement, cytokine, vasodilatory, and lymphatic inflammatory response produces raised sharply demarcated erythema, warmth, edema, tenderness, induration, lymphangitis, and regional nodes.

Local superficial infection can produce fever, chills, malaise, tachycardia, leukocyte response, high CRP, PCT rise in severe disease, hypotension, lactate elevation, AKI, delirium, and rare organ dysfunction.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Bullous, hemorrhagic, and superficial necrotic vascular leak
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Toxin-mediated inflammation, capillary leak, superficial vessel injury, edema pressure, host fragility, or delayed control can produce vesicles, bullae, blood-filled blisters, purpura, erosions, and superficial necrosis without necessarily implying deep fascial necrosis.

Lymphedema, prior lymph node dissection, venous insufficiency, chronic edema, obesity, previous erysipelas, or recurrent lymphangitis weakens local clearance and increases edema, extent, recurrence, and slow resolution.

Advanced age, diabetes, CKD, peripheral vascular disease, cirrhosis, malignancy, transplant, corticosteroids, biologics, immunosuppressants, HIV, neutropenia, or malnutrition impair containment and alter pathogen spectrum.

A small subset develops bacteremia, septic shock, or metastatic foci such as endophthalmitis, pericarditis, or other sterile-site inflammation. These are event hazards, not separate labels inside the disease name.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Inactive, delayed, or poorly delivered antimicrobial effect
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Delay, premature discontinuation, wrong spectrum for host/pathogen context, allergy-limited therapy, underdosing, renal dosing errors, poor tissue delivery in edematous or ischemic skin, or missed local care prolong burden and complications.

Hazard that a deep necrotizing soft tissue infection is present or evolving; warning axis for rapidly progressive pain, hemorrhagic bullae, necrosis, shock, gas, or deep fascial signs.

Lifespan outcome hazard from erysipelas; very low in uncomplicated superficial disease, rising with septic shock, bacteremia, atypical Gram-negative/immunosuppressed host, AKI, delayed active therapy, necrotizing mimic hazard, and severe comorbidity.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Border and erythema extent are correlated visual features of the same plaque but should not cause each other.
Warmth and pain track local inflammatory intensity.
Chronic edema makes acute edema larger and more persistent.
Chronic lymphatic compromise is a major recurrence driver.
Portal evidence increases probability that a superficial bacterial inoculation explains the plaque.
Bullae can evolve into serohematic or hemorrhagic bullae in severe superficial disease.
Hemorrhagic bullae require active exclusion of necrotizing infection while remaining compatible with bullous erysipelas.
CRP and WBC often co-rise but may dissociate in immunosuppression.
Very high PCT in an immunosuppressed host can support severe bacterial or Gram-negative context.
Hypotension and vasopressor-dependent shock increase AKI hazard.
Shock is the main path from erysipelas to mortality.
Metastatic infection raises mortality and morbidity hazard.

Edema magnifies swelling and extent.
Chronic lymphatic impairment drives recurrence.

Portal strength increases entry mechanism.

Severe infection is less tolerated.

Chronic wounds and ulcers create portals.

Atypical and Gram-negative pathogens are more plausible in severe immune compromise.

Hemorrhagic bullae and necrosis demand parallel necrotizing-mimic assessment.
Bullae, erosions, or necrotic surface injury may need wound care.

Delayed active therapy prolongs pathogen burden and local injury.
Delay worsens severe complicated disease.

supportive_care: Serially document lesion border, raised edge, erythema extent, warmth, edema, tenderness, induration, lymphangitic streaking, lymphadenopathy, bullae, purpura, necrosis, pain trajectory, and spread rate.

Assess portals and recurrence contexts: tinea pedis, toe-web maceration, trauma, insect bite, piercing, surgical scar, ulcer, chronic edema, lymphedema, venous insufficiency, obesity, diabetes, PAD, immunosuppression, and prior erysipelas.
Use CBC with differential, CRP/ESR, creatinine/BUN, electrolytes, lactate when unstable, and procalcitonin when severe bacterial sepsis or atypical pathogen context is being assessed.

Image only when depth, abscess, DVT, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, necrotizing fasciitis, foreign body, or unusual anatomic complication is uncertain. Superficial fat stranding supports but does not define the disease.

Keep blood culture species, blister/wound culture species, susceptibility, NGS, biopsy exclusion, final source adjudication, and response to therapy as confirmatory/post-workup context unless the test mode explicitly includes them.

Treat shock physiology with fluids, vasopressors, oxygen or ventilation, renal support, glucose/electrolyte management, and ICU monitoring while antimicrobial and source-control vectors address the infection.

For bullous or hemorrhagic erysipelas, protect the skin barrier, manage ruptured bullae/erosions, monitor for necrotizing mimics, and avoid letting superficial necrosis alone relabel the disease as necrotizing fasciitis without deep evidence.

After acute control, reduce recurrence by edema control, compression when vascular status permits, limb elevation, skin care, tinea/intertrigo treatment, wound care, weight/venous management, and selected antimicrobial prophylaxis in recurrent high-risk contexts.

Do not force erysipelas to win by deleting true mimic evidence. Cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, diabetic foot infection, toxic shock syndrome, sepsis, bacteremia leaves, SJS-TEN/DRESS, zoster, DVT, septic arthritis, and carcinoma erysipeloides remain legitimate competitors when their own observed evidence is present.
